doc.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010

title: Youngstown State, Tony Leonardi and Sal Nistico
summary: LaLama's mentor Tony Leonardi started the jazz band at Youngstown State and brought Sal Nistico in; Nistico later put him on gigs in New York. The talk turns to Upstate Italian-American players.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: That’s right. Come between Rochester — you know I have, I don’t know if this is part of the question but I’m going to say it here — I have an affinity here for Upstate New York because I’m from Pittsburgh and I’ve been living in New York for about 35 years. But I grew up in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. And I went to school at Youngstown State University. And why that’s relevant is there was a guy that was going to school at the time, he just got off of Woody Herman’s band, his name was Tony Leonardi. And he was from Syracuse, okay. So he grew up with Sal [Amico], he played with Chuck [Mangione] and you know he played with Joe Romano and Nick and probably J.R. too. But Tony was kind of my mentor, you know. Even though he was about eleven years older than me. And at Youngstown State he started which was at that time a one hour elective jazz band. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

It wasn’t part of the curriculum really except for it was an elective. So my point is that Tony turned me on to all kinds of great, you know he heard I played — I auditioned for the band. I didn’t know the band. I just auditioned for the band, I made it, and we started becoming with friends, and he turned me on to all these hip — then I remember he invited Sal Nistico to the school, so we could hear him, you know? And he played with us, and then I got to know Sal. Now again when I moved to New York I moved to Queens, Elmhurst Queens. And at that time Sal lived in Rego Park. And Sal was nice enough, you know, because he remembered me and he knew I was trying to play and all that stuff, and so he put me on some of his gigs, you know, like quartet gigs, he made them a quintet for little Ralphie to play. You know what I mean? Right out of school, I was in my early twenties. Because I got out of Woody Herman’s band and Sal was there, and Tony Leonardi played — you know I didn’t play with him, I mean in Woody’s band, but I mean they were alumni. Joe Romano. I met Joe, coming to New York, and then Nick I played with up here. So the only one I didn’t know that well was J.R. because he was already gone playing when I started. So I always feel like, not that this is my home, but I always felt like very close to the Upstate guys because of Tony, and then Sal, and then Joe you know, and even Chuck.
And all these Upstate guys are, you know their last name always ends with a vowel.
Well that’s it: Lovano, LaLama, you know, Nistico. Even Zito or a’s.
Very interesting. A couple of books have come out recently about that. Italian Americans in the jazz world.
That’s right. That’s true. Most definitely.
